implementation_notes: Rust's stdlib gives the claim directly: HashSet::insert returns true only when the value was newly inserted, so a Mutex<HashSet<_>> (or a DashMap for sharded contention) makes check-and-claim one operation and there is no separate lock discipline to get wrong. It remains process-local, so a scaled-out or restart-prone receiver needs the durable variant; unwrap() on a poisoned lock should be replaced by an explicit policy in production.
pitfalls: Mutex poisoning after a panicking holder makes every later claim fail; decide explicitly whether to recover or fail the receiver.
A HashSet has no TTL - sweep by age or move retention into the store.
Holding the lock guard across the effects turns the guard into a global serialization point; claim, drop the guard, then process.

variants.name: Durable claim with a unique index (sqlx)
variants.implementation_notes: The durable realization inserts the claim into a table with a UNIQUE key inside the same transaction as the effects: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING` with rows_affected() == 1 is the claim, and sqlx surfaces the affected-row count on the query result. Prefer it for any receiver whose duplicates can outlive a process, and prune rows older than the redelivery window.
pitfalls: Only the claim statement's affected-row count is meaningful; reuse the same transaction for the effects but check n first.
A connection or constraint error must return as a failure for redelivery, never as 'already processed'.
